canonical_statement: The review aimed to estimate the 1-year relative effects of dapagliflozin versus other oral anti-diabetes treatments when added to metformin monotherapy.
The study combined a systematic literature review with a Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

The initial systematic search was conducted in May 2011 across EMBASE, MEDLINE, CENTRAL, conference proceedings, trial registries, reference lists, and manufacturer-provided unpublished dapagliflozin reports.
Electronic databases, registries, and key conference proceedings were updated in October 2012, and studies were not excluded by language.
Study filtering and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers.
Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials of 52 weeks plus or minus 6 weeks in adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin monotherapy.

population.label: Adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin monotherapy
inclusion_criteria: Metformin monotherapy background with inadequate glycaemic control

canonical_statement: Shorter trials and long-term extensions of trials shorter than 52 weeks were excluded from the primary evidence network because early treatment effects might not persist and extension phases could introduce selection bias.

canonical_statement: The network considered licensed add-on classes including sulphonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, meglitinides, and GLP-1 analogues; alpha-glucosidase inhibitors were excluded from scope.
HbA1c efficacy was defined as mean change from baseline at approximately 1 year.

canonical_statement: Hypoglycaemia was analysed as the proportion with at least one episode; when multiple definitions were reported, the broadest definition was selected and trial definitions were categorized by severity, symptoms, and biochemical confirmation.

outcome.definition: Proportion of subjects experiencing at least one episode of hypoglycaemia using each trial authors' definition; the broadest reported definition was selected when multiple definitions were available

canonical_statement: Where variance data were missing, the review attempted prognostic imputation from trial arms in the same drug class; adjusted mean changes were extracted when trial authors reported them.
Indirect comparisons used sulphonylureas as the common comparator, with agents and licensed doses pooled within drug class according to prespecified decisions.
HbA1c and weight were modelled with a normal likelihood on a linear scale, while hypoglycaemia was modelled on an odds-ratio scale.
Both fixed- and random-effects models were reported; the random-effects model was selected a priori for the base analysis because heterogeneity across RCTs was expected.

A network-level baseline-HbA1c covariate model was fitted for HbA1c; the adjustment coefficient was -0.02 percentage points with a 95% credible interval from -0.23 to 0.24 and did not support effect modification.
Two GLP-1 studies using an intensive diet and exercise regimen with a 600-kcal daily deficit were excluded post hoc from the base case and retained for sensitivity analysis.
The searches identified 4270 abstracts, 2882 after deduplication, eight studies meeting inclusion criteria, and six RCTs in the primary network.

population.label: Systematic-review study flow: 4270 identified, 2882 deduplicated, 8 included, 6 primary-analysis RCTs

canonical_statement: All six primary-analysis RCTs were actively controlled with a sulphonylurea, producing a star-shaped evidence network with sulphonylureas as the common comparator.
Across primary-analysis RCTs, mean baseline HbA1c ranged from 7.3% to 8.7% and mean baseline weight from 84 to 93 kg.

canonical_statement: The validity of the network meta-analysis depends on exchangeability of relative effects across contributing trials; differences in populations, design, dosing/titration, and outcome definitions could violate this assumption.
The evidence network was small: individual pairwise comparisons contributed only one to four RCTs, requiring a common between-study variance structure to support random-effects estimation.
Although baseline HbA1c was examined as an effect modifier, the influence of unknown confounders could not be tested quantitatively.
Specific safety outcomes other than hypoglycaemia were not meta-analysed because adverse-event reporting was class-specific and inconsistent across trials.
The literature search was updated through October 2012; subsequently available evidence, including a canagliflozin trial, was outside the review coverage.
The study was funded by Bristol-Myers Squibb and AstraZeneca.

Multiple authors were employees and/or stockholders of Bristol-Myers Squibb, AstraZeneca, or Oxford Outcomes, and A. H. Barnett reported honoraria/advisory relationships with several pharmaceutical companies.

The authors concluded that after 1 year, dapagliflozin added to metformin offered similar HbA1c control to licensed comparator classes, with similar or reduced hypoglycaemia risk and additional weight loss.
Supporting Appendix S1 provides the detailed electronic database search strategies used for the systematic review, including EMBASE and Ovid MEDLINE search terms and randomized-trial filters.
